criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1 (Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8): The paper is a political-ecology study of agro-industrial land and raw water resource 'grabs' (surface and groundwater irrigation extraction and pollution) by the sugarcane and ethanol biofuel sector in Valle del Cauca, Colombia, rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Although it cites secondary watershed concession shares (p. 9) and briefly notes in two anecdotal passages (p. 11) that agro-industrial extraction contributes to dry-season municipal supply shortages and forces some displaced smallholders to buy household water, it does not study a household or community water/sanitation service system.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper examines governance and regulatory arrangements—specifically the Bonsucro voluntary multi-stakeholder sustainability certification scheme for sugarcane ethanol, Colombian biofuel mandates, and Cauca Valley Corporation (CVC) bulk irrigation concessions and raw-water potability classifications—so C2 in isolation would be satisfied on a literal broad reading, though the overall study still would be excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = 'exclude') because it studies agricultural/industrial biofuel resource grabs rather than household water/sanitation service access (Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, C2 is 'no': private biofuel commodity certification metrics (net irrigation/mill water per kg of cane/sugar/ethanol and plantation land title) and agro-industrial irrigation resource concessions are not rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules for service, household tariffs, disconnection/enforcement, or utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3: Empirical qualitative case study drawing on 14 in-depth exploratory interviews conducted between June and August 2012 with sugarcane/ethanol industry stakeholders in Valle del Cauca, additional interviews with rural community residents, and analysis of Bonsucro standard documents and secondary regional reports.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear/indirect for review scope: The primary outcomes examined are agro-industrial land concentration, irrigation water resource capture, and industry framing/adaptation of prospective Bonsucro certification standards. Secondary watershed concession shares (64% surface water and 88% groundwater held by the sugar industry vs. 26% and 2% for household use) and brief anecdotal accounts of dry-season municipal shortages and displaced rural residents buying water for household use are mentioned (pp. 9, 11), but no household/community water service-access outcome is systematically evaluated in relation to a service-governance mechanism.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails C5 for review scope: While the qualitative stakeholder sample (n = 14) and biofuel certification exposure are identifiable for the agro-industrial case study, the paper does not define an identifiable household/community service-user sample, service-governance exposure, and household water/sanitation service-access outcome (and Bonsucro certification was still in pre-audit/training stages rather than empirically linked to household water access).
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6: Full text is in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: More recently, critics have pointed out that land grabs are also closely associated with ‘‘water grabs,’’ that is efforts to secure existing surface and ground water resources (Mehta et al. 2012).

Bonsucro (2013) is the principal MSI that focuses on sustainability standards for sugar and sugarcane ethanol production. Launched in 2005, the brand Bonsucro was not established until 2010 and certiﬁcation began in 2011.

The standard does not address the sugar industry’s legacy in the Valle del Cauca of disproportionate water concessions, lower water prices and high rates of contamination, as discussed above, and like the land case, these historical factors are invisible in Bonsucro.
The paper draws on in-depth exploratory interviews with 14 stakeholders in the sugarcane and ethanol industry in the Valle del Cauca region in southwest Colombia between June and August 2012.
They described the difﬁculties they now face in accessing water for household use, and how they are forced to buy water for household use.

raw_response.exposure: Bonsucro voluntary multi-stakeholder sustainability certification standards for sugar and sugarcane ethanol production, alongside national biofuel mandates/incentives and regional Cauca Valley Corporation (CVC) agricultural water concessions
raw_response.outcome: Prospects for Bonsucro certification adoption and legitimation of agro-industrial land concentration and irrigation water resource capture, with secondary watershed concession shares and brief anecdotal mentions of dry-season municipal supply shortages and displaced rural residents buying water for household use
raw_response.population_and_sample: 14 stakeholders in the sugarcane and ethanol industry in the Valle del Cauca region (farmers, union activists, local government officials, sugar industry association officials, sugar refineries, and research agronomists), plus an unspecified number of rural community residents interviewed between June and August 2012
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see also Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8 on water-resource and industrial water-access studies). This qualitative political-ecology study examines how voluntary transnational biofuel sustainability certification (Bonsucro) and national biofuel incentives interact with historical land concentration and agro-industrial irrigation 'water grabs' in Colombia's sugarcane ethanol sector. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service delivery or a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing household/community service access (only noting in passing that agro-industrial river/aquifer extraction contributes to dry-season municipal shortages and forces some displaced smallholders to buy household water). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because its subject is agricultural/industrial biofuel certification and raw natural-resource capture rather than water or sanitation service access.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative exploratory case study (in-depth stakeholder interviews and document/secondary data analysis)
